patient.name: Graham Whitfield
patient.complaint: Three weeks of puffy eyes, swollen legs and frothy urine

diagnosis.exam: Expect 'Which is the most likely diagnosis?' with oedema, a normal JVP and labs showing heavy proteinuria and low albumin, or 'most likely cause' picked by age, anti-PLA2R or HIV.

steps.lead: Graham's filter is leaking: the barrier has failed, so **albumin** spills into his urine.

steps.lead: Graham's oedema is **low oncotic pressure**; his cholesterol of 9.4 is the liver over-compensating.

steps.q: Why is Graham at high risk of DVT and renal vein thrombosis?
o: Loss of vitamin K in urine
steps.r: Antithrombin III is small enough to leak out, while the liver makes **more clotting factors**: a hypercoagulable state.

Minimal change has **no immune complexes**; a T-cell permeability factor flattens foot processes, so steroids work well.
Graham's ramipril works inside the kidney: **efferent dilation** lowers glomerular pressure and proteinuria.

steps.text: Low total T4 in nephrotic syndrome is lost **thyroid-binding globulin**, not true hypothyroidism.

mcq.r: Triad: **proteinuria >3.5 g/day, hypoalbuminaemia, hyperlipidaemia**. The others are nephritic.

o: Efferent arteriole dilation lowers glomerular pressure

glossary.Nephrotic syndrome: Kidney disorder with heavy proteinuria, low albumin, high lipids and oedema.
glossary.Nephritic syndrome: Glomerular inflammation causing haematuria, red cell casts, hypertension and reduced renal function.
glossary.Hyperlipidaemia: Raised fats such as cholesterol in the blood.
glossary.Anasarca: Severe generalised oedema affecting the whole body.
glossary.Lipiduria: Fat in the urine, seen as fatty casts or oval fat bodies.
glossary.Minimal change disease: Commonest childhood cause of nephrotic syndrome; normal on light microscopy, responds to steroids.
glossary.Membranous nephropathy: Commonest adult cause of nephrotic syndrome; anti-PLA2R antibodies form subepithelial immune deposits.
glossary.FSGS: Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis: scarring of parts of some glomeruli, classically linked to HIV.
glossary.Anti-PLA2R: Autoantibody against the phospholipase A2 receptor on podocytes; marker of membranous nephropathy.
glossary.GBM: Glomerular basement membrane, part of the kidney's filtration barrier.
glossary.Podocyte: Cell wrapping the glomerular capillaries with foot processes that form the filtration slit.
glossary.Effacement: Flattening of podocyte foot processes, seen on electron microscopy.
glossary.Subepithelial: Between the GBM and the podocytes, where membranous immune deposits sit.
glossary.Immune complex: Antibody bound to antigen, which can deposit in tissues and cause inflammation.
glossary.Oncotic pressure: Pull of plasma proteins, mainly albumin, that keeps fluid inside blood vessels.
glossary.Antithrombin III: Natural anticoagulant protein lost in nephrotic urine, causing a clotting tendency.
glossary.Renal vein thrombosis: Clot in the renal vein causing flank pain and haematuria; classic in membranous nephropathy.
glossary.Hypercoagulable: More likely than normal to form blood clots.
glossary.VTE: Venous thromboembolism: DVT or pulmonary embolism.
glossary.DVT: Deep vein thrombosis, usually in the leg.
glossary.PE: Pulmonary embolism: a clot blocking the lung arteries.
glossary.Thyroid-binding globulin: Protein carrying thyroid hormone; lost in urine, lowering total T4.
glossary.PCR: Urine protein:creatinine ratio, a spot test that quantifies proteinuria.
glossary.ACR: Urine albumin:creatinine ratio, a spot test that quantifies albuminuria.
glossary.Renal biopsy: Taking a core of kidney tissue to examine the glomeruli; gold standard.
glossary.ACE inhibitor: Drug such as ramipril that blocks angiotensin II formation, lowering BP and proteinuria.
glossary.ARB: Angiotensin receptor blocker such as losartan; alternative to an ACE inhibitor.
glossary.Efferent arteriole: Vessel carrying blood out of the glomerulus; dilating it lowers glomerular pressure.
glossary.Furosemide: Loop diuretic used to clear oedema.
glossary.Prednisolone: Oral corticosteroid; first-line for minimal change disease.
glossary.Ciclosporin: Calcineurin inhibitor immunosuppressant; second-line for steroid-resistant minimal change disease.
glossary.LMWH: Low molecular weight heparin, a subcutaneous anticoagulant.
glossary.Enoxaparin: A low molecular weight heparin used for thromboprophylaxis.
glossary.Steroid-resistant: Disease that does not remit after an adequate course of steroids.
glossary.JVP: Jugular venous pressure; raised in fluid overload from heart failure.
glossary.ELISA: Lab antibody test, used here to screen for HIV.
glossary.SLE: Systemic lupus erythematosus, an autoimmune disease that can cause membranous nephropathy.
glossary.URTI: Upper respiratory tract infection, such as a cold.

technique.stem: A 64 year old man has 4 weeks of progressive leg swelling and frothy urine. He takes amlodipine for hypertension. His BP is 132/84 mmHg. His JVP is not raised. He has pitting oedema to the knees and dullness at both lung bases. Urine dipstick shows protein 4+ and no blood. Serum albumin is 16 g/L and total cholesterol 9.1 mmol/L.
technique.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

steps.x: Diagnosis question with oedema: decide where the fluid comes from (heart, liver, kidney).
Frothy urine and 4+ protein = protein loss. Low albumin and high cholesterol complete the **triad**. No blood rules out nephritic.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Heavy proteinuria + low albumin + high lipids + oedema: **nephrotic syndrome**.

elim: The JVP is not raised; heavy proteinuria and low albumin point to the kidney.
Nephritic gives haematuria and hypertension; this dipstick has no blood.
Can cause swelling and high cholesterol, but not 4+ proteinuria.
Causes ankle oedema but not proteinuria, low albumin or effusions.

steps.x: **C. Nephrotic syndrome.** Pulmonary signs and ankle oedema do not mean heart failure: check the urine and the albumin.

technique.stem: A 47 year old woman has 2 weeks of swollen ankles and puffy eyes in the mornings. She is otherwise well. Her BP is 124/78 mmHg. She has pitting oedema to mid-shin. Her heart sounds are normal and her chest is clear.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?

steps.x: 'Initial' investigation: the first, quickest test, not the gold standard.
Periorbital oedema in the morning with a normal heart suggests **protein loss** from the kidney.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Check the urine for protein at the bedside: **dipstick**, then quantify with PCR.

elim: Her chest is clear; it would not explain the oedema.
No cardiac features; periorbital oedema points to protein loss.
The gold standard, but not first: confirm proteinuria first.
Does not show proteinuria; it is not the first test.

steps.x: **E. Urine dipstick.** Initial = dipstick; quantify = PCR/ACR; gold standard = biopsy.

technique.stem: A 55 year old man has membranous nephropathy confirmed on renal biopsy. His BP is 142/90 mmHg. His urine protein:creatinine ratio is 520 mg/mmol (<15). He is on furosemide for oedema. He wants to reduce the protein leaking into his urine.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate drug to add?

steps.x: Management: the goal named is less proteinuria, not just BP.
Nephrotic-range proteinuria in a confirmed nephrotic patient; the question asks to cut the leak.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **ACE inhibitor** (or ARB): efferent dilation lowers glomerular pressure.

elim: Lowers BP but has no specific antiproteinuric effect.
Alpha-blocker; no effect on intraglomerular pressure.
Lowers BP but not proteinuria in the same way.
Rate-limiting calcium channel blocker; not used to cut proteinuria.

steps.x: **C. Lisinopril.** Proteinuria in nephrotic syndrome = ACE inhibitor or ARB.

technique.stem: A 42 year old woman with nephrotic syndrome has a serum albumin of 14 g/L. She develops a swollen, painful left calf and a deep vein thrombosis is confirmed on ultrasound. She has no personal or family history of clots.
technique.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of her thrombosis?
o: Antithrombin III loss in the urine
Reduced hepatic synthesis of clotting factors

steps.x: Science question: explain why a nephrotic patient clots.
Very low albumin means a heavy leak; small proteins like **antithrombin III** leak too.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Antithrombin III lost in the urine plus more hepatic clotting factors.

elim: Inherited; there is no family history and a clear acquired cause.
Also inherited; nothing suggests it.
The opposite: the liver makes more clotting factors.
Low platelets cause bleeding, not clots.

steps.x: **A. Antithrombin III loss in the urine.** Nephrotic VTE = antithrombin III loss; that is why they get LMWH.

practice.stem: A 66 year old man has 3 weeks of progressive ankle swelling. He has a history of hypertension treated with amlodipine. His temperature is 36.6°C, pulse rate 78 bpm, BP 128/82 mmHg and oxygen saturation 97% breathing air. His JVP is not raised. He has bilateral pitting oedema to the thighs and dullness at both bases. Urine microscopy shows no cells and no casts.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Oedema with PCR 590, albumin 15 and high cholesterol, no casts and a normal JVP, is nephrotic syndrome. Nephritic needs haematuria and casts.

steps.x: Diagnosis: oedema with lab results; decide heart, liver or kidney.
Normal JVP, bland sediment, effusions: look at the labs for the **triad**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: PCR 590, albumin 15, cholesterol 9.2: **nephrotic syndrome**.

elim: The JVP is normal and the labs show protein loss.
Normal liver features; the urine is full of protein.
No red cells or casts; BP is normal.
Creatinine is normal and there is no haematuria.

steps.x: **D. Nephrotic syndrome.** Effusions do not mean heart failure: check albumin and urine protein.

practice.stem: A 5 year old boy is brought to the GP with puffy eyes for 4 days. His mother says his ankles are now swollen. He had a cold 10 days ago. His BP is normal. Urine dipstick shows protein 4+ and no blood. Serum albumin is 18 g/L.
practice.q: Which is the most likely underlying cause?
practice.e: Minimal change disease is the commonest cause of nephrotic syndrome in children, classically after a viral URTI. Post-streptococcal GN is nephritic with haematuria.

steps.x: Asks for the underlying cause: name the glomerular disease.
Young child, periorbital oedema, heavy protein, no blood, after a viral URTI.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Nephrotic syndrome in a child after a cold: **minimal change disease**.

elim: Mainly adults and linked to HIV.
Commonest in White adults, not young children.
Nephritic: haematuria, high BP, cola urine.
Nephritic picture with falling renal function.

steps.x: **C. Minimal change disease.** Child + URTI + nephrotic = minimal change.

practice.stem: A 61 year old White man has nephrotic syndrome. He has no diabetes, takes no regular medicines and has no rash or joint pains. His BP is 134/82 mmHg. Blood tests show positive anti-PLA2R antibodies and his HIV test is negative.
practice.q: Which is the most likely underlying cause?
practice.e: Anti-PLA2R antibodies are the signature of primary membranous nephropathy, the commonest cause in White adults. FSGS is linked to HIV.

steps.x: Underlying cause of nephrotic syndrome in an adult.
White adult with **anti-PLA2R**: the antibody is the signature.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Membranous nephropathy.

elim: He does not have diabetes.
Linked to HIV; his test is negative.
No rash or joint symptoms; anti-PLA2R points elsewhere.
A childhood disease with no antibody marker.

steps.x: **D. Membranous nephropathy.** Anti-PLA2R = membranous nephropathy.

practice.stem: A 52 year old woman with membranous nephropathy has sudden severe right flank pain and visible haematuria. She is not febrile. Her pulse rate is 98 bpm, BP 134/82 mmHg and respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute. Her serum albumin is 15 g/L. She is not on thromboprophylaxis.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Membranous nephropathy has the highest risk of renal vein thrombosis, presenting with flank pain and haematuria. She is afebrile, so pyelonephritis is unlikely.

steps.x: Diagnosis of a new event in a known nephrotic patient: think complication.
Membranous disease, very low albumin, no LMWH, then flank pain and haematuria.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Renal vein thrombosis**, the classic membranous complication.

elim: She is afebrile; nothing suggests infection.
Presents slowly with weight loss, not sudden pain.
Usually from AF emboli; her hypercoagulable state points to the vein.
Colicky loin-to-groin pain; no link to her low albumin.

steps.x: **D. Renal vein thrombosis.** Nephrotic + flank pain + haematuria = renal vein thrombosis.

practice.stem: A 39 year old man with nephrotic syndrome has sudden breathlessness and sharp right-sided chest pain worse on breathing in. His temperature is 37.1°C, pulse rate 118 bpm, BP 118/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 91% breathing air. His chest is clear on auscultation.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Nephrotic syndrome is hypercoagulable, so sudden pleuritic pain, tachycardia and hypoxia with a clear chest is PE. Pneumonia needs fever and focal signs.

steps.x: Diagnosis of an acute event in a nephrotic patient.
Sudden pleuritic pain, tachycardia and hypoxia with a clear chest in a hypercoagulable state.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Pulmonary embolism** from antithrombin III loss.

elim: No orthopnoea or crackles; the chest is clear.
No fever or focal signs.
Breath sounds would be reduced on one side.
Would not explain the hypoxia and tachycardia in a hypercoagulable patient.

steps.x: **D. Pulmonary embolism.** Breathless nephrotic patient = PE until proven otherwise.

practice.stem: A 34 year old man has 6 weeks of leg swelling. He was diagnosed with HIV 2 years ago and does not take his antiretroviral therapy. Investigations show urine protein:creatinine ratio 710 mg/mmol (<15) and serum albumin 17 g/L (35–50). Urine dipstick shows no blood.
practice.q: Which is the most likely underlying cause?
practice.e: FSGS is the HIV-associated cause of nephrotic syndrome. Membranous is commoner in White adults overall but the HIV is the deciding clue.

steps.x: Underlying cause: use the background.

clues: does not take his antiretroviral therapy
steps.x: Untreated **HIV** plus nephrotic-range proteinuria.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: FSGS, most commonly caused by HIV.

elim: Gives visible haematuria after infection; there is no blood.
Commonest in White adults, but HIV points elsewhere.
Mainly children after a viral URTI.
Nephritic with haematuria and high BP.

steps.x: **A. Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis.** HIV + nephrotic = FSGS.

practice.stem: A 58 year old woman has nephrotic syndrome. She has a urine protein:creatinine ratio of 610 mg/mmol (<15), serum albumin 18 g/L (35–50) and cholesterol 8.8 mmol/L (<5.0). Her pulse rate is 76 bpm and BP 130/80 mmHg. The team need to establish the underlying glomerular disease.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?
practice.e: Renal biopsy is the gold-standard investigation that shows the glomerular lesion. Anti-PLA2R supports membranous nephropathy but does not replace histology.

steps.x: 'Diagnostic' and 'underlying glomerular disease': the gold standard.
The triad is already confirmed; now they need the **histology**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Renal biopsy, the definitive gold standard.

elim: Quantifies protein; the PCR already does this.
Supports membranous nephropathy but does not confirm the lesion.
Does not show glomerular histology.
Shows kidney size and obstruction, not the glomerulus.

steps.x: **D. Renal biopsy.** To confirm the cause: renal biopsy.

practice.stem: A 50 year old man has 3 weeks of ankle and facial swelling. His pulse rate is 80 bpm and BP 136/84 mmHg. Urine dipstick shows protein 4+ and no blood or leucocytes. His GP wants to quantify the proteinuria.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate next investigation?
practice.e: A urine protein:creatinine ratio quantifies proteinuria on a spot sample after a positive dipstick. Biopsy finds the cause but does not quantify.

steps.x: 'Quantify the proteinuria' is the key phrase.
Dipstick has screened positive; now measure the amount.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Urine PCR** (or ACR).

elim: Gold standard for the cause, but not to quantify protein.
Shows the consequence, not the amount of protein lost.
No leucocytes; this is not an infection.
Looks for cells and casts; it does not measure protein.

steps.x: **E. Urine protein:creatinine ratio.** Dipstick screens, PCR quantifies.

practice.stem: A 6 year old girl has periorbital and ankle oedema 1 week after a viral sore throat. Urine dipstick shows protein 4+ and no blood. Serum albumin is 16 g/L. Her pulse rate is 96 bpm and BP 98/62 mmHg. Minimal change disease is suspected.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
practice.e: Minimal change disease responds very well to steroids, so prednisolone is first-line. Ciclosporin is reserved for steroid-resistant disease.

steps.x: Initial management of a named cause.
Child, after a URTI, nephrotic: minimal change disease.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Steroids**: oral prednisolone.

elim: Second-line, for steroid-resistant disease.
Helps oedema but does not treat minimal change.
Reduces proteinuria but is not the first-line treatment here.
Reserved for relapsing or resistant disease, not first-line.

steps.x: **C. Prednisolone.** Minimal change: prednisolone first, ciclosporin if steroid-resistant.

practice.stem: A 7 year old boy has minimal change disease. Despite an adequate course of oral prednisolone, he still has protein 4+ on dipstick and serum albumin 19 g/L (35–50). His BP is 100/64 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
practice.e: Ciclosporin is the second-line treatment for steroid-resistant minimal change disease. Furosemide and albumin only manage oedema.

steps.x: 'Next step' after first-line failed.

clues: Despite an adequate course of oral prednisolone
steps.x: Steroid-resistant minimal change disease.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Second-line: **ciclosporin**.

elim: Treats oedema only, not the disease.
Used in lupus, not minimal change.
Temporary; does not induce remission.
Reduces proteinuria but is not the second-line agent for steroid resistance.

steps.x: **A. Ciclosporin.** Steroid-resistant MCD = ciclosporin.

practice.stem: A 57 year old woman is admitted with membranous nephropathy and gross oedema. Her pulse rate is 84 bpm and BP 134/80 mmHg. She has limited mobility. Her eGFR is 72 mL/min/1.73m².
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate thromboprophylaxis?
practice.e: Antithrombin III loss makes nephrotic syndrome hypercoagulable, so prophylactic LMWH such as enoxaparin is given. Aspirin does not prevent venous thrombosis adequately.

steps.x: Management: which drug prevents clots in this patient.
Very low albumin, membranous disease and immobility: very high VTE risk.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **LMWH (enoxaparin)** prophylaxis.

elim: Antiplatelet; does not prevent venous clots well enough.
Not enough with this degree of hypercoagulability.
Her risk of VTE and renal vein thrombosis is high.
Antifibrinolytic; it promotes clotting.

steps.x: **B. Enoxaparin.** Nephrotic with low albumin = prophylactic LMWH.

practice.stem: A 45 year old man has nephrotic syndrome with gross pitting oedema and ascites. His pulse rate is 80 bpm, BP 128/80 mmHg and JVP is not raised. His serum albumin is 13 g/L (35–50).
practice.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of his oedema?
practice.e: Hypoalbuminaemia lowers plasma oncotic pressure so fluid moves into the interstitium. A normal JVP argues against raised right atrial pressure.

steps.x: Science: explain the oedema.
Very low albumin with a normal JVP.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Less albumin = **low oncotic pressure**; fluid moves into the interstitium.

elim: Would cause ascites with hepatomegaly, not generalised oedema.
Seen in sepsis and burns, not here.
Gives non-pitting localised oedema.
The JVP is not raised.

steps.x: **E. Reduced plasma oncotic pressure.** Nephrotic oedema = low oncotic pressure.
